questions.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
options: The mass of a bag of rice: 50 kg
The temperature of the lecture hall: 28 °C
The time a lecture lasts: 90 minutes
The velocity of a trotro: 60 km/h towards Madina
questions.exp: A vector needs a magnitude and a direction. Mass, temperature and time are fully described by a number and a unit.
questions.ref: Deck: Scalars and vectors

questions.q: Kofi walks once around a circular track and returns to his starting point. Which statement is correct?
options: His displacement is zero, but the distance he walked is not zero.
His displacement and his distance are both zero.
His displacement is not zero, because he walked a long way.
His displacement equals the distance he walked, because both are lengths.
questions.exp: Displacement is a vector from start to finish. Start and finish are the same point, so it is zero. Distance is a scalar that adds up the whole path.
questions.ref: Deck: Displacement: a vector from start to finish

questions.q: A student says, "A temperature of −10 °C is a vector because it is negative." What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong. Every negative quantity is a vector.
Temperature is a vector only when it is below zero.
A negative sign on a scalar is not a direction in space. A vector needs a direction in space.
Temperature is a vector only if it is measured in kelvin.
questions.exp: Scalars can be positive, negative or zero. The sign tells us about the value, not about a direction in space.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: scalar or vector?

questions.q: A taxi driver in Accra says, "I am 3 km from Madina." Why is this not enough to find the taxi?
options: A distance cannot be measured in kilometres.
A distance is a scalar. It gives the size but not the direction.
A distance is a vector, so it needs a unit vector.
3 km is too large to be a displacement.
questions.exp: Knowing only how far, with no direction, leaves a whole circle of possible positions. A displacement gives both magnitude and direction.
questions.ref: Deck: Scalars and vectors

questions.q: Which pair contains one scalar and one vector?
options: Mass and energy
Distance and time
Displacement and force
Speed and velocity
questions.exp: Speed is the magnitude of velocity and is a scalar. Velocity has a direction and is a vector. In the other pairs, both quantities are of the same kind (scalars, scalars, vectors).
questions.ref: Deck: Scalars and vectors

questions.q: A force is a vector. What does this tell us about a force of 10 N?
options: It is not completely described until we also give its direction.
It is completely described by the number 10 and the unit N.
It can be negative only if the force is pulling.
It can be added to another force by adding the two numbers 10 and 5, whatever the directions.
questions.exp: A vector needs a magnitude, a unit and a direction. Vectors add by their directions as well as their sizes.
questions.ref: Deck: Magnitude and direction

questions.q: What is the difference between A and A (or |A|)?
options: They mean the same thing. The bold type is only decoration.
A is the magnitude and A is the direction.
A is the vector, with magnitude and direction. A is its magnitude, a non-negative number with a unit.
A is the vector and A is always a unit vector.
questions.exp: We write the vector in bold (or with an arrow) and its magnitude in ordinary type. Mixing them up causes errors in later topics.
questions.ref: Deck: Notation: vector and magnitude

questions.q: Which statement can never be true for the magnitude |A| of a vector?
questions.exp: A magnitude is a length. It is zero or positive, never negative. Only a component can be negative.
questions.ref: Deck: Notation: vector and magnitude

questions.q: Two vectors A and B are drawn as arrows of the same length and the same direction, one starting at Legon gate and the other at Madina. How are A and B related?
options: They are different vectors, because their starting points differ.
They are equal only if they start from the same point.
They are equal in magnitude but not in direction.
They are equal vectors. A vector is defined by its magnitude and direction, not by where it starts.
questions.exp: We can slide a vector parallel to itself without changing it. This is what makes head-to-tail addition possible.
questions.ref: Deck: Representing a vector

questions.q: What does the vector −A look like compared with A?
options: The same length, pointing in the opposite direction
The same direction, with a negative length
A shorter arrow in the same direction
The same length, perpendicular to A
questions.exp: Multiplying a vector by −1 reverses its direction and keeps its magnitude.
questions.ref: Deck: Subtracting vectors

questions.q: What happens to the vector A when it is multiplied by the scalar 3?
options: It becomes three times longer and rotates by 3°.
It stays the same length and points three times further round.
It becomes three times longer and keeps the same direction.
It becomes a scalar.
questions.exp: Multiplying a vector by a positive scalar changes its magnitude only. A negative scalar would also reverse the direction.
questions.ref: Deck: Representing a vector

questions.q: What is the difference between the magnitude of a vector and a component of that vector?
options: They are the same thing in different units.
The magnitude is the length of the whole vector and is never negative. A component is the part along one axis and can be positive, negative or zero.
A component is always larger than the magnitude.
The magnitude can be negative, but a component cannot.
questions.exp: Components depend on the axes we choose. The magnitude does not.
questions.ref: Deck: What is a component?

questions.q: A vector has components A<sub>x</sub> = −3 and A<sub>y</sub> = 0 (in metres). Which statement is correct?
options: The vector is zero, because A<sub>y</sub> is zero.
The vector lies along the y-axis.
The vector has a negative magnitude.
The vector lies along the x-axis, pointing in the −x direction.
questions.exp: A zero component means no part of the vector lies along that axis. The negative sign on A<sub>x</sub> gives the direction along x.
questions.ref: Deck: Signs and quadrants

questions.q: Can a component of a vector be larger than the magnitude of the vector?
options: No. A component is at most as large as the magnitude.
Yes, whenever the component is negative.
Yes, if the angle is larger than 45°.
Yes, if the axes are rotated far enough.
questions.exp: A component is the vector's length times a cosine or sine, and these lie between −1 and +1.
questions.ref: Deck: Resolving a vector into components

questions.q: If we rotate the x and y axes but leave the vector unchanged, what happens?
options: The magnitude changes, but the components do not.
Both the components and the magnitude change.
The components change, but the magnitude does not.
Nothing changes.
questions.exp: The vector is a physical thing. Components describe it relative to chosen axes, so they depend on the choice. The length of the arrow does not.
questions.ref: Deck: Graphs build understanding; components let us calculate

questions.q: Why can the component A<sub>x</sub> of a vector be negative while the magnitude A cannot?
options: The component is measured in different units.
The component carries a direction along the axis, and the magnitude is just a length.
The component is always the smaller number.
Negative numbers are used only for scalars.
questions.exp: The sign of a component tells us which way along the axis the vector points. A length cannot be negative.
questions.ref: Deck: What is a component?

questions.q: A vector lies exactly along the +y axis. What are its components?
options: A<sub>x</sub> = A and A<sub>y</sub> = 0
A<sub>x</sub> = A and A<sub>y</sub> = A
A<sub>x</sub> = 0 and A<sub>y</sub> = 0
A<sub>x</sub> = 0 and A<sub>y</sub> = A, its magnitude
questions.exp: All of the vector lies along y and none along x.
questions.ref: Deck: Resolving a vector into components

questions.q: The resultant of two vectors is the single vector that has the same effect as both. Does the order of addition matter, that is, is A + B equal to B + A?
options: Yes, they are equal. Vector addition is commutative.
No, A + B points opposite to B + A.
No, but they have the same magnitude.
It depends on the angle between the vectors.
questions.exp: Both orders give the same diagonal of the parallelogram, so addition does not depend on order.
questions.ref: Deck: Adding two vectors: three equivalent ways

questions.q: Is vector subtraction commutative, that is, is A − B equal to B − A?
options: Yes, they are always equal.
No, they differ in magnitude but have the same direction.
No. They have the same magnitude but point in opposite directions.
Yes, but only when the vectors are perpendicular.
questions.exp: B − A = −(A − B). Reversing the order reverses the direction.
questions.ref: Deck: Subtracting vectors

questions.q: How do we subtract a vector, as in A − B?
options: Subtract the magnitude of B from the magnitude of A, and keep the direction of A
Add the vector −B to A
Rotate B by 90° and add it to A
Add B to A and reverse the result
questions.exp: Subtraction is addition of the opposite vector. It is not a subtraction of magnitudes unless the vectors lie along one line.
questions.ref: Deck: Subtracting vectors

questions.q: Two vectors have magnitudes 3 and 4. A student says the magnitude of their sum is always 7. When is the student right?
options: Always, because 3 + 4 = 7
Only when the vectors are perpendicular
Only when the vectors point in opposite directions
Only when the vectors point in the same direction
questions.exp: Magnitudes add only along one line. For other angles the magnitude of the sum is smaller than 7.
questions.ref: Deck: Predicting the resultant: along one line

questions.q: Two displacements, 3 km east and 4 km north, are added. Which statement about the resultant is correct?
options: Its magnitude is less than 7 km, and it points between east and north.
Its magnitude is 7 km, and it points north-east at 45° whatever the sizes.
Its magnitude is 1 km, because the vectors are perpendicular.
It points east, because 3 km east is the first displacement.
questions.exp: The two legs are not along one line, so the sides of the triangle do not simply add. The resultant is the shortest route from the start to the finish.
questions.ref: Deck: Perpendicular vectors: Pythagoras

questions.q: When three or more vectors are added by the head-to-tail method, which statement is correct?
options: The resultant depends on which vector is drawn first.
The resultant is the sum of the three magnitudes.
The resultant is the same whichever order we draw them in.
The resultant always points along the longest vector.
questions.exp: Vector addition is both commutative and associative. The order changes the drawing, not the resultant.
questions.ref: Deck: Three or more vectors: the order does not matter

questions.q: In the head-to-tail method, where does the resultant vector start and end?
options: It starts at the head of the first vector and ends at the tail of the last vector.
It starts at the tail of the first vector and ends at the head of the last vector.
It starts where the two heads meet.
It joins the heads of the two longest vectors.
questions.exp: The resultant goes straight from where we started to where we finished, which is what we mean by displacement.
questions.ref: Deck: Adding two vectors: three equivalent ways

questions.q: After adding vectors, a student gets a resultant with a negative magnitude. What should the student conclude?
options: The resultant points opposite to the first vector.
The result is correct if the angle is large.
The resultant is a scalar.
A mistake has been made, since a magnitude is never negative.
questions.exp: Magnitude is a length. A negative value means the sign of a component or a difference has been confused with the magnitude.
questions.ref: Deck: Notation: vector and magnitude

questions.q: What is the largest possible magnitude of A + B for given magnitudes A and B, and when does it happen?
options: A + B, when the vectors are parallel
A + B, when the vectors are perpendicular
|A − B|, when the vectors are parallel
A + B, when the vectors are antiparallel
questions.exp: Parallel vectors point the same way, so their magnitudes simply add.
questions.ref: Deck: Rules: parallel, antiparallel, and the bounds on R

questions.q: What is the smallest possible magnitude of A + B for given magnitudes A and B, and when does it happen?
options: Zero, always
A + B, when the vectors are antiparallel
|A − B|, when the vectors are antiparallel
|A − B|, when the vectors are parallel
questions.exp: Antiparallel vectors point in opposite directions, so the larger one partly cancels the smaller. The result is zero only if A = B.
questions.ref: Deck: Rules: parallel, antiparallel, and the bounds on R

questions.q: What does the word antiparallel mean?
options: The vectors are perpendicular to each other.
The vectors lie along the same line but point in opposite directions.
The vectors have opposite magnitudes.
The vectors point in the same direction.
questions.exp: Antiparallel is an angle of 180° between the vectors. Parallel is 0°.
questions.ref: Deck: Rules: parallel, antiparallel, and the bounds on R

questions.q: Which statement about the magnitude of A + B is true for any angle between the vectors?
options: It is always equal to A + B.
It is always larger than A + B.
It is always smaller than |A − B|.
It always lies between |A − B| and A + B.
questions.exp: The two extreme cases are antiparallel (smallest) and parallel (largest). Every other angle gives a value in between.
questions.ref: Deck: Rules: parallel, antiparallel, and the bounds on R

questions.q: A vector A is added to a vector antiparallel to it, of larger magnitude. Which way does the resultant point?
options: The same way as the larger vector
The same way as A
Perpendicular to both
It has no direction, because the vectors cancel
questions.exp: The larger vector wins. Only when the magnitudes are equal does the resultant become the zero vector.
questions.ref: Deck: Predicting the resultant: along one line

questions.q: Two vectors have the same magnitude and are antiparallel. What is their sum?
options: Twice the magnitude of either vector
The scalar zero, which is not a vector
The zero vector
A vector perpendicular to both
questions.exp: Equal and opposite vectors cancel completely. Note that the zero vector has zero magnitude and no particular direction.
questions.ref: Deck: Predicting the resultant: along one line

questions.q: A vector points up and to the left, in the second quadrant. What are the signs of its components?
options: A<sub>x</sub> is positive and A<sub>y</sub> is positive.
A<sub>x</sub> is negative and A<sub>y</sub> is positive.
A<sub>x</sub> is positive and A<sub>y</sub> is negative.
A<sub>x</sub> is negative and A<sub>y</sub> is negative.
questions.exp: The sign of each component tells which way along that axis the vector points. Left is negative x and up is positive y.
questions.ref: Deck: Signs and quadrants: predict first

questions.q: A vector points down and to the left, in the third quadrant. What are the signs of its components?
options: Both components are positive.
A<sub>x</sub> is positive and A<sub>y</sub> is negative.
A<sub>x</sub> is negative and A<sub>y</sub> is positive.
Both components are negative.
questions.exp: Left is −x and down is −y. Predicting the signs from a sketch before using a calculator catches many errors.
questions.ref: Deck: Signs and quadrants: predict first

questions.q: A vector makes an angle of 30° with the x-axis in the fourth quadrant (below the axis, on the right). What are the signs of its components?
options: A<sub>x</sub> is positive and A<sub>y</sub> is negative.
A<sub>x</sub> is negative and A<sub>y</sub> is positive.
Both are positive, because 30° is positive.
Both are negative, because the vector points downwards.
questions.exp: The angle being a positive number does not make both components positive. The quadrant decides each sign.
questions.ref: Deck: Signs and quadrants: predict first

questions.q: In the usual formulas A<sub>x</sub> = A cos θ and A<sub>y</sub> = A sin θ, what is θ?
options: The angle between the vector and the y-axis
Always the acute angle the vector makes with the nearest axis
The angle measured from the +x axis, anticlockwise to the vector
The angle between the vector and the horizontal, whatever the axes
questions.exp: The formulas hold for the angle from +x, anticlockwise. If the angle is measured from another axis, cosine and sine may swap.
questions.ref: Deck: Resolving a vector into components

questions.q: A vector makes an angle α with the y-axis. Which component is A sin α?
options: A<sub>y</sub>, the component along the y-axis
A<sub>x</sub>, the component perpendicular to the y-axis
Neither component. It is the magnitude.
The component in the z direction
questions.exp: The side opposite the angle is A sin α. When the angle is measured from y, the component along y uses cosine and the x-component uses sine.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 4: angles measured from other axes

questions.q: A student resolves a vector and finds that both components are larger than the vector's magnitude. What should the student do?
options: Accept it, since components can be larger than the vector.
Take the square root of each component.
Add the two components to get the magnitude.
Check the work, because each component must be no larger than the magnitude.
questions.exp: The magnitude is √(A<sub>x</sub>² + A<sub>y</sub>²), at least as large as either component. This is a quick reasonableness check.
questions.ref: Deck: Resolving a vector into components

questions.q: Two students resolve the same vector with different axes. One gets A<sub>x</sub> = 4 and the other gets A<sub>x</sub> = 3. Is it possible that both are correct?
options: Yes, if they chose axes with different orientations.
No. A component is a fixed property of the vector.
Yes, but only if one of them made an arithmetic error.
No. The components must always agree.
questions.exp: Components describe the vector relative to a set of axes. Different axes give different components for the same vector.
questions.ref: Deck: Graphs build understanding; components let us calculate

questions.q: A calculator gives tan⁻¹(A<sub>y</sub>/A<sub>x</sub>) = 30° for a vector with A<sub>x</sub> < 0 and A<sub>y</sub> < 0. What must we do?
options: Nothing. The calculator always gives the correct direction.
Change the sign of the answer and use −30°.
Check the quadrant. The vector is in the third quadrant, so the direction is not 30° from +x.
Use 30° and swap the sign of A<sub>x</sub>.
questions.exp: The inverse tangent cannot tell opposite quadrants apart, because the ratio of two negatives is the same as the ratio of two positives. A sketch of the components fixes the quadrant.
questions.ref: Deck: Direction from components: a common error

questions.q: What does "30° north of east" mean?
options: Start by pointing north, then rotate 30° towards east.
Start by pointing east, then rotate 30° towards north.
30° from the north pole.
A direction 30° to the south of east.
questions.exp: The direction word after "of" is the starting axis. "North of east" is closer to east than to north.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 4: angles measured from other axes

questions.q: What is the difference between "30° north of east" and "30° east of north"?
options: They are the same direction.
They are opposite directions.
One is a vector and the other is a scalar.
They are different directions, because the angle is measured from different axes.
questions.exp: 30° north of east lies 30° from east. 30° east of north lies 30° from north, which is 60° from east. The word after “of” is the axis we start from.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 4: angles measured from other axes

questions.q: Why do we need the quadrant, as well as the reference angle, to state the direction of a vector?
options: The reference angle alone is not enough. We also need the quadrant to say which way the vector points.
The quadrant is not needed if the magnitude is known.
The reference angle is always measured from the y-axis.
The magnitude decides the quadrant.
questions.exp: Four different directions share the same reference angle. The signs of the components identify the quadrant.
questions.ref: Deck: Reconstructing: magnitude, reference angle, quadrant, direction

questions.q: Two different vectors have the same magnitude. Which statement is correct?
options: They must be equal vectors.
They must be parallel.
They may point in different directions, so the vectors may be different.
They must point in opposite directions.
questions.exp: A vector needs both magnitude and direction. Equal magnitude alone does not make two vectors equal.
questions.ref: Deck: Magnitude and direction

questions.q: If both components of a vector are doubled, what happens to the vector?
options: Its magnitude stays the same and its direction rotates.
Its magnitude doubles and its direction stays the same.
Its magnitude doubles and its direction doubles.
Its direction reverses.
questions.exp: Doubling both components scales the vector by 2. The ratio A<sub>y</sub>/A<sub>x</sub>, and so the direction, is unchanged.
questions.ref: Deck: Two equivalent descriptions of one vector

questions.q: What is a unit vector?
options: A vector measured in metres
A vector whose components are all equal
A vector with a magnitude of one metre, one second or one kilogram
A vector of magnitude one, used to show a direction, with no units
questions.exp: A unit vector is dimensionless. Its job is to point. We multiply it by a number with units to build a vector.
questions.ref: Deck: Unit vectors and the 3D Cartesian system

questions.q: In the expression A = Ax î + Ay ĵ, what does î do?
options: It shows the +x direction and has magnitude one.
It multiplies the vector by the number i.
It shows the magnitude of A.
It rotates the vector by 90°.
questions.exp: The unit vector gives the direction, A<sub>x</sub> gives how much, and the sign of A<sub>x</sub> gives which way along x.
questions.ref: Deck: Unit vectors and the 3D Cartesian system

questions.q: The unit vector Â of a vector A is found by dividing A by its magnitude. What does Â tell us?
options: The size of A only
Both the size and the direction of A
Only the direction of A
The angle between A and the x-axis only
questions.exp: Dividing by the magnitude removes the size, and what remains is a pure direction of magnitude one.
questions.ref: Deck: The unit vector of a vector

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the unit vector ĵ?
options: Zero
One, with no units
One metre
It depends on the vector it is attached to
questions.exp: Unit vectors have magnitude 1 and no dimensions.
questions.ref: Deck: Unit vectors and the 3D Cartesian system

questions.q: A vector is written as A = −5 î. What is its direction?
options: The +x direction, because the magnitude is positive
The +y direction
It has no direction
The −x direction
questions.exp: A negative number multiplying a unit vector reverses the direction. The magnitude of A is still 5.
questions.ref: Deck: Unit vectors and the 3D Cartesian system

questions.q: Which statement about the unit vectors î, ĵ and k̂ is correct?
options: They are mutually perpendicular.
They are all parallel.
They all point in the +x direction.
They are perpendicular only when the axes are rotated.
questions.exp: They point along the three Cartesian axes, which are at right angles to one another.
questions.ref: Deck: Unit vectors and the 3D Cartesian system

questions.q: In spherical coordinates, what is the polar angle θ?
options: The angle measured from the +x axis in the xy-plane
The angle between the vector and the xy-plane
The angle measured from the +z axis to the vector
The angle between the vector and its own projection
questions.exp: The polar angle runs from 0° (along +z) to 180° (along −z).
questions.ref: Deck: Components of a vector in 3D

questions.q: In spherical coordinates, what is the azimuthal angle φ?
options: The angle measured from the +z axis to the vector
The angle in the xy-plane, measured from +x to the projection of the vector
The angle between the vector and the z-axis
The angle between two vectors
questions.exp: It is the longitude-like angle. It runs from 0° to 360°.
questions.ref: Deck: Components of a vector in 3D

questions.q: A vector lies in the xy-plane. What is its polar angle θ?
options: It cannot be defined.
questions.exp: The polar angle is measured from +z. A vector lying flat in the xy-plane is at a right angle to z.
questions.ref: Deck: Components of a vector in 3D

questions.q: A vector points along +z. What can we say about its azimuthal angle?
options: It is not defined, because the vector has no projection in the xy-plane.
It is 90°.
It is 180°.
It is 360°.
questions.exp: With no projection in the xy-plane, there is no direction in the plane to measure from x. The polar angle is 0°.
questions.ref: Deck: Components of a vector in 3D

questions.q: What range of values can the polar angle θ take?
questions.exp: From the +z axis to the −z axis. The azimuthal angle is the one that goes through 360°.
questions.ref: Deck: Components of a vector in 3D

questions.q: What kind of quantity is the dot product A·B?
options: A vector perpendicular to both A and B
A scalar, a single number with a unit but no direction
A vector in the plane of A and B
A unit vector
questions.exp: The dot product is also called the scalar product because its result has no direction.
questions.ref: Deck: The dot (scalar) product

questions.q: What is A·A?
options: The zero vector
Zero
Twice the magnitude of A
The square of the magnitude of A
questions.exp: The angle between a vector and itself is 0° and cos 0° = 1, so A·A = A². This is a scalar and it is not zero unless A = 0.
questions.ref: Deck: The dot (scalar) product

questions.q: When is the dot product of two non-zero vectors equal to zero?
options: When they are perpendicular
When they are parallel
When they are antiparallel
Never, because both are non-zero
questions.exp: A·B = AB cos φ is zero when cos φ = 0, that is φ = 90°.
questions.ref: Deck: Sign of the dot product, and which angle is φ

questions.q: The dot product of two vectors is negative. What does this tell us?
options: The vectors are perpendicular.
One of the vectors has a negative magnitude.
The angle between the vectors, tail to tail, is greater than 90°.
The vectors are parallel.
questions.exp: cos φ is negative for φ between 90° and 180°. Magnitudes are never negative, so the sign comes only from the cosine.
questions.ref: Deck: Sign of the dot product, and which angle is φ

questions.q: The dot product A·B is positive and as large as possible. What can be said about A and B?
options: They are perpendicular.
They are parallel.
They are antiparallel.
They have equal magnitudes.
questions.exp: The largest value, AB, comes when cos φ = 1, that is φ = 0°.
questions.ref: Deck: Sign of the dot product, and which angle is φ

questions.q: Is the dot product commutative, that is, is A·B equal to B·A?
options: No, they differ by a sign.
No, they are perpendicular to each other.
Only when the vectors are parallel.
Yes, they are always equal.
questions.exp: A B cos φ is the same whichever vector we write first.
questions.ref: Deck: The dot (scalar) product

questions.q: Which angle is used for φ in A·B = AB cos φ?
options: The angle between the vectors when they are placed tail to tail
The angle at the head of the head-to-tail triangle
The angle measured from the x-axis
Always an acute angle
questions.exp: Using the inside angle of a head-to-tail triangle gives the supplementary angle, and the sign of the dot product comes out wrong.
questions.ref: Deck: Sign of the dot product, and which angle is φ

questions.q: What does the dot product tell us physically, when one of the vectors is a force and the other a displacement?
options: The torque of the force
The direction in which the object will turn
How much of the force acts along the displacement, which gives the work done
The direction of the net force
questions.exp: Work is force along the displacement times the displacement. Only the component of the force along the motion contributes.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: What kind of quantity is the cross product A×B?
options: A scalar
A vector, perpendicular to both A and B
A vector in the same plane as A and B
A unit vector
questions.exp: The cross product is also called the vector product. Its direction comes from the right-hand rule.
questions.ref: Deck: The cross (vector) product: geometry first

questions.q: What is A×A?
options: The square of the magnitude of A
A vector perpendicular to A, with magnitude A²
The number 1
The zero vector
questions.exp: The angle between a vector and itself is 0° and sin 0° = 0, so the magnitude is zero. The result is a zero vector, not the number zero.
questions.ref: Deck: Using the right-hand rule

questions.q: Is the cross product commutative, that is, is A×B equal to B×A?
options: No. They have the same magnitude but point in opposite directions.
Yes, they are always equal.
No. They have different magnitudes.
Yes, but only if the vectors are perpendicular.
questions.exp: B×A = −A×B. Reversing the order reverses the direction given by the right-hand rule.
questions.ref: Deck: Common mistakes in Contact B

questions.q: When is the cross product of two non-zero vectors the zero vector?
options: When they are perpendicular
Only when they are parallel
When they are parallel or antiparallel
Never
questions.exp: |A×B| = AB sin φ is zero when φ = 0° or 180°.
questions.ref: Deck: Using the right-hand rule

questions.q: When is the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors as large as possible?
options: When they are parallel
When they are perpendicular
When they are antiparallel
When they have the same magnitude
questions.exp: The largest value, AB, comes when sin φ = 1, that is φ = 90°.
questions.ref: Deck: The cross (vector) product: geometry first

questions.q: What is the direction of A×B?
options: Along A
Along the resultant A + B
Halfway between A and B
Perpendicular to the plane of A and B, given by the right-hand rule
questions.exp: Curl the fingers of the right hand from the first vector towards the second. The thumb points along the product.
questions.ref: Deck: Using the right-hand rule

questions.q: With the usual right-handed axes, what is î×ĵ?
options: k̂
ĵ
The number 1
questions.exp: Curling the fingers from +x to +y, the thumb points along +z.
questions.ref: Deck: Cross products of the unit vectors

questions.q: With the usual right-handed axes, what is î×î?
options: î
k̂
The zero vector
The number 1
questions.exp: The angle between î and î is 0° and sin 0° = 0.
questions.ref: Deck: Cross products of the unit vectors

questions.q: Torque is defined by τ = r×F. What kind of quantity is torque?
options: A scalar
A vector, perpendicular to the plane of r and F
A vector along F
A vector along r
questions.exp: Because torque is a cross product, it is a vector, and the order of r and F matters.
questions.ref: Deck: Torque: the cross product in physics

questions.q: A mechanic pushes on a spanner. Which push turns the nut most effectively, for the same force?
options: A push along the spanner
A push at 0° to the spanner
A push at 180° to the spanner
A push perpendicular to the spanner
questions.exp: The torque has magnitude rF sin φ. Only the part of the force perpendicular to r turns the nut.
questions.ref: Deck: Torque: the cross product in physics

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches each product with its type of result?
options: Dot product: scalar. Cross product: vector.
Dot product: vector. Cross product: scalar.
Both are vectors.
Both are scalars.
questions.exp: This is the main reason for the names scalar product and vector product.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: For two perpendicular vectors, which statement is correct?
options: The dot product has its largest value and the cross product is zero.
Both products are zero.
The dot product is zero and the cross product has its largest magnitude.
Both products have their largest values.
questions.exp: cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: For two parallel vectors, which statement is correct?
options: The dot product is zero and the cross product has its largest value.
The dot product has its largest value and the cross product is zero.
Both are zero.
Both have their largest values.
questions.exp: cos 0° = 1 and sin 0° = 0.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: Which product changes sign when we swap the order of the vectors?
options: The dot product only
Both products
Neither product
The cross product only
questions.exp: The dot product is commutative. The cross product is anticommutative: A×B = −B×A.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: A student needs to find how much of a force acts along a displacement. Which product is suitable?
options: The dot product
The cross product
Neither, because the components cannot be combined
Either, since they give the same result
questions.exp: The dot product picks out the part of one vector along another. The cross product picks out the part perpendicular.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: What is the difference between A·A and A×A?
options: Both are equal to A².
Both are the zero vector.
A·A is the scalar A². A×A is the zero vector.
A·A is the zero vector. A×A is the scalar A².
questions.exp: The angle between a vector and itself is zero, so cos is 1 and sin is 0.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: The dot product of two vectors equals the product of their magnitudes. What is the cross product's magnitude?
options: The same product of magnitudes
Zero
Half of that product
It cannot be found without the angle
questions.exp: The dot product equals AB only when cos φ = 1, so φ = 0° and sin φ = 0. The angle is known from the statement.
questions.ref: Deck: Dot product and cross product compared

questions.q: A student writes "A·B = C" with C a vector. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since the dot product of two vectors is a vector.
The dot product has no unit.
The dot product must be zero.
The dot product is a scalar, so it cannot equal a vector.
questions.exp: Both sides of an equation must be the same kind of quantity. A scalar cannot equal a vector.
questions.ref: Deck: Common mistakes in Contact B

questions.q: A student writes the distance as 25 and forgets the unit. Why does this matter?
options: A number without a unit is not a physical quantity, and the answer cannot be checked.
It does not matter, since the number is the physics.
It matters only for vectors.
It matters only for scalars.
questions.exp: The unit is part of the quantity. Units also allow a quick check that the formula was used correctly.
questions.ref: Deck: Before vectors: units and significant figures

questions.q: Which of these cannot be a correct way of writing a force?
options: 25 kg m/s²
questions.exp: The metre is a unit of length. The newton, kg m/s² and kN are all units of force.
questions.ref: Deck: Before vectors: units and significant figures

questions.q: Two vectors can be added only if they represent the same kind of physical quantity. Which sum makes sense?
options: A displacement plus a force
A displacement plus a displacement
A force plus a velocity
A velocity plus a mass
questions.exp: Adding quantities with different dimensions has no physical meaning.
questions.ref: Deck: Magnitude and direction

questions.q: Which of these is the dimension of the dot product of a force and a displacement?
options: The dimension of force only
The dimension of length only
Dimensionless
Force times length, the dimension of energy
questions.exp: The dot product multiplies the magnitudes (with the cosine), so the units multiply: N·m = J.
questions.ref: Deck: The dot (scalar) product

questions.q: What are the units of a unit vector?
options: None. It is dimensionless.
Metres
Newtons
The same as the vector it comes from
questions.exp: We divide the vector by its own magnitude, so the units cancel.
questions.ref: Deck: The unit vector of a vector

questions.q: A cross product of a position (m) and a force (N) is calculated. What are the units of the result?
options: N
m
N·m, the unit of torque
N/m
questions.exp: The units of a product multiply, as with the magnitude of any cross product.
questions.ref: Deck: Torque: the cross product in physics

questions.q: A student converts a speed from km/h to m/s by multiplying by 1000 and by 3600. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong.
The conversion factor for hours is wrong. It should divide by 3600, since there are 3600 seconds in an hour.
The student should have used 60 instead of 3600.
The conversion cannot be done.
questions.exp: Write the factors as ratios equal to 1 and check that the unwanted units cancel. 1 km/h = 1000 m / 3600 s.
questions.ref: Deck: Before vectors: units and significant figures

questions.q: A measured length is written as 2.40 m. What does the trailing zero tell us?
options: The zero is not important and can be dropped.
The length is exactly 2.4 m.
The length is known to the nearest metre.
The length is known to the nearest 0.01 m.
questions.exp: A zero after the decimal point is a significant figure. It shows the precision of the measurement.
questions.ref: Deck: Before vectors: units and significant figures

questions.q: A calculator shows 3.8461538 for a result found by dividing two numbers measured to three significant figures each. What should we report?
options: 3.85, with three significant figures
3.8461538, since the calculator is more accurate
4, with one significant figure
3.846, with four significant figures
questions.exp: The result cannot be more precise than the least precise input. Extra digits from the calculator carry no meaning.
questions.ref: Deck: Before vectors: units and significant figures

questions.q: Two lengths are added: 12.5 m and 0.25 m. Which rule applies to the sum?
options: Keep the number of significant figures of the most precise term.
Keep all the digits the calculator shows.
Keep the number of decimal places of the least precise term.
Multiply the precision of the terms.
questions.exp: For addition and subtraction, we count decimal places. For multiplication and division, we count significant figures.
questions.ref: Deck: Before vectors: units and significant figures

questions.q: Which of the following is a reason not to round intermediate results in a long calculation?
options: Rounding is not allowed in physics.
Rounding early can accumulate error in the final answer.
Intermediate results have no units.
Calculators round automatically.
questions.exp: Keep extra digits during the calculation, and round only the final answer to the right number of significant figures.
questions.ref: Deck: How good is a measured value?
